source_read: PDF, online-first version (pp. 1–8, as printed on that version; print Psychological Medicine 53: 987–994): all pages; Tables 1–4 and Fig. 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; a relative risk for the never vs past-only comparison recomputed from Table 4; Supplementary Tables S1–S3 not available.

key_findings.note: The categories are not monotonic (1.37, then 1.32, then 2.85); see missed.
'Assuming causality' is in the Methods' PAF paragraph (p. 3); the locator could add it.

reporting_issues.note: The Methods' confounder list (p. 2) has no IQ measure.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E is the right instrument. Overall high agreed: ROBINS-E allows high when several domains with some concerns together substantially lower confidence, and here they bear on an estimate whose lower limit is 1.03, with an E-value of 1.57. 'Some concerns' would also be defensible; I side with high.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: Some concerns agreed, with a case for high: other illicit drug use (only cannabis and alcohol adjusted) and earlier psychotic experiences (no lagged outcome in the models) are not controlled, and adjusting for concurrent depression, anxiety and life stress may remove part of an effect. These run in opposite directions, so I would not raise the domain.

Add to the note: at ages 18, 21 and 25 the symptom window was the past month while use covered the years since the previous interview (p. 2), so exposure and outcome windows differ in three of five waves; the paper says the difference was corrected in the analyses without saying how.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it substantial rather than minor (a judgment to log for the senior author). The card's five gaps are right, and together they change what a reader takes away: the abstract presents the at-least-weekly odds ratio as if it came from the model with concurrent cannabis use; its conclusion that risk is confined to regular and recent use, and that there is no persistent vulnerability without continued use, rests on Table 4, which groups people by any use, where the never vs past-only difference is imprecise rather than absent (see missed); and the closing sentence upgrades self-reported symptom items, reported at the same interviews as use, to 'an independent risk factor for psychosis'.

missed: Exposure and outcome windows differ (p. 2): use was asked for the period since the previous interview at every wave, symptoms for the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25 and since the previous assessment only at 30 and 35; the abstract describes both as covering the period since the previous interview (p. 1). The card repeats the abstract's description in design_detail ('for the periods since the previous interview'), cannot_establish ('reported for the same interval') and abstinence_at_testing ('reported for the same period'); these should say that use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews over different windows at the first three.

Never vs past-only comparison at ages 30–35 (Table 4): it is not tested separately, and the counts reconstructed from the percentages (34 of 672 and 16 of 215) give a relative risk of about 1.47 (95% CI about 0.83 to 2.6; editors' calculation). The data do not exclude a moderate lasting excess, so the abstract's 'no evidence for a persistent vulnerability' is an absence of evidence.

The dose–response categories are not monotonic (Table 3: 1.37 for once or twice, 1.32 for up to about monthly, 2.85 for at least weekly), so the pattern is a contrast between at least weekly use (51 people) and the rest, not a gradient; relevant to any dose–response upgrade.
Table 3's heading gives the frequency window as ages 18–35, while the text calls it lifetime (16–35) (pp. 6–7). Minor.
